source.title: Dataset distillation for memorized data: Soft labels can leak held-out teacher knowledge

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. One sentence in Section 5.3 has a redacted teacher accuracy (“XX%”), so that specific value is unavailable.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends the random-label memorization setting to knowledge distillation: it trains students on teachers’ soft labels and measures recovery of held-out teacher-memorized examples, including on random i.i.d. data and random sequences. It does not directly reproduce the original random-label training experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. for fitting completely random labels, but that cited result is not a row. Rows below cover the paper’s own random i.i.d. teacher/student experiments and the related modular-addition setting. No result tests fitting shuffled pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs as in V3, label-noise interpolation in V4, explicit regularization in V5, or the real-label-before-noise claim in V6.
record.test_reason: The student distillation results measure a different outcome, but the paper also reports its own teachers' training accuracy on independent random labels and Gaussian inputs. Those teacher results bear on V1 and the Gaussian-input part of V3; the record omits them as separate rows.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: teacher soft labels transfer information about held-out memorized examples through statistical leakage or functional teacher recovery. Transfer depends on temperature, capacity, and data availability. Exact teacher recovery was not obtained in the GPT-2 experiment.
record.recipe_differences: This is a distillation study: teacher models are trained on finite data, then students are trained from teacher soft labels on a subset. The paper cites the original random-label memorization result but does not reproduce direct random-label training.
record.method_sensitivity: Leakage and teacher matching depend strongly on softmax temperature, student training fraction, sample complexity, model capacity and architecture; the structured-data outcomes also depend on whether the teacher has generalized.

fits_no_version.finding: Students recover held-out teacher-memorized random labels through soft labels, sometimes perfectly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Teacher soft labels can transmit information about memorized examples absent from the student's training inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: On modular addition, soft-label transfer depends on temperature and teacher generalization, and can prevent students from discovering task structure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distillation can transfer a teacher's memorized predictions separately from the task's generalizing structure.

record.problems: The evidence uses synthetic random data, a structured modular-addition task, and one GPT-2 instance on synthetic sequences; authors say the relevance to natural distributions and deeper architectures remains unclear. The teacher accuracy in the GPT-2 section is redacted as “XX%.” Several results are described qualitatively without numerical values in the text, and some supplementary capacity sweeps are reported as single runs.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure-only sweeps without text-described outcome values were not transcribed as separate numerical rows.

untested.parts: No matched true-label experiment establishes unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters. Independent-data chance accuracy is principally established by the random-data construction rather than a numerical teacher validation result in the prose.
No comparison of fitting times for true and random labels, or convergence across corruption fractions.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and comparison with the same networks on ordinary inputs.
No interpolation from clean to completely corrupted labels or corresponding test-error curve.
No relevant regularization ablation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
No temporal comparison of learning real patterns and noisy labels. Memorizing soft labels before matching a teacher function measures a different distinction.

missing.what: Separate teacher training-accuracy rows: p = 500 ReLU networks perfectly memorize n = 25,000 and 100,000 Gaussian-input examples with independent random labels.
missing.locator: Section 5 setup; Section 5.2, Figure 5 and caption

missing.what: Teacher capacity failures at high sample complexity, including the n = 200,000 example; distinguish teacher accuracy from student recovery.
Direct random-label teacher fitting reaches 100% in the two-dimensional illustrative experiments; widths are p = 100 for three classes and p = 300 for twenty classes.
missing.locator: Figure 1 caption; Appendix A, Figure 8 caption

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's blanket V1 limits_scope verdict on student distillation. An untested direct-training condition is not a scope limitation. Existing rows receive cannot_determine relative to the claim versions; their reported transfer effects can still be observed for the separate claims described under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Tests whether students can fit held-out random labels indirectly from teacher soft labels; does not test direct fitting of completely random labels by standard stochastic-gradient training or test error at chance for that direct training.

rows.subject: binary logistic regression
rows.operation_detail: Student weights recovered by pseudo-inverse from teacher logits on its training partition; measured held-out accuracy as sample complexity varied.
rows.measure: Student accuracy on held-out teacher-memorized examples
rows.note: This is student recovery via teacher logits, not direct random-label training. The paper reports the threshold value approximately and describes held-out recovery as perfect.
rows.check: Pseudo-inverse recovery of held-out teacher labels by logistic regression measures transfer of memorized information, not random-label fitting by a deep network.
